summary: The note surveys local wetland restoration and protection efforts that have emerged since September 2023, covering flood control, wildlife recovery, fisheries, and new legislation. It profiles projects and leaders such as Dr. Lillian Harrow, Martin Blake, Dr. Rachel Aguirre, Captain Jim O'Reilly and Assembly Member Gabriela Torres. It concludes that despite challenges like invasive species and industrial opposition, community engagement, science and policy make recovery promising.
one_line: Local wetland restoration projects, led by scientists, fishers and legislators, are boosting flood protection, wildlife, livelihoods and policy, though challenges remain.
key_facts: Wetlands provide water filtration, flood protection, and carbon storage, and support many flora and fauna.
The New Dawn Wetlands Project, led by Dr. Lillian Harrow, aims to revive over 500 acres of degraded wetland on the outskirts of Greater Marshville.

The New Dawn project was celebrated around World Wetlands Day on February 2, 2024, and involves water control structures and reintroduction of native plant species lost to industrial pollution and unsanitary runoff.
The Riverside Wetlands Project began operations in May 2024, created by hydrologist Martin Blake and the Riverside Conservancy, and has helped reduce flood damage in neighboring townships.
Martin Blake says properly functioning wetlands absorb a tremendous amount of stormwater and that savings in potential property damage justify restoration investment.
The Greentail Wetlands, restored in late 2023, have become a hotbed for birdwatchers and nature enthusiasts.
Dr. Rachel Aguirre reports the return of bird species such as the marsh harrier and the bittern, which are key indicators of a healthy wetland.
Dr. Rachel Aguirre, with the National Wildlife Federation, organizes workshops for local schools on the importance of wetlands.
The Turnaround Fisheries Project, led by Captain Jim O'Reilly, began in summer 2024 and proposed restrictions on certain fishing practices and pollution controls in critical wetland areas.
Fishers in the Turnaround Fisheries Project have reported a marked increase in fish populations and water clarity.
The Wetlands Preservation Act of 2025, championed by Assembly Member Gabriela Torres, provides for wetland health assessment, protected status for critical areas, and penalties for harmful land use.
Torres says the act incentivizes green infrastructure and penalizes pollution.
Challenges to recovery include invasive species and apathy or opposition from certain industrial stakeholders.
